{{Short description|Unit conversion factor in physics}}
{{DISPLAYTITLE:''g''<sub>c</sub> (engineering)}}

In [[engineering]] and [[physics]], '''''g''<sub>c</sub>''' is a unit [[conversion of units#Conversion factors|conversion factor]] used to convert [[mass]] to [[force]] or vice versa.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Janna |first1=William |year=2015 |title=Introduction to Fluid Mechanics |publisher=[[CRC Press]] |isbn=9781482211610 |page=5 |edition=5th}}</ref> It is defined as
:<math>g_\text{c} = \frac{ma}{F}</math>

In unit systems where force is a [[derived unit]], like in [[SI unit]]s, ''g''<sub>c</sub> is equal to 1. In unit systems where force is a primary unit, like in [[imperial and US customary measurement systems]], ''g''<sub>c</sub> may or may not equal 1 depending on the units used, and value other than 1 may be required to obtain correct results.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Cengel |first1=Yunus |last2=Boles |first2=Michael |year=2014 |title=Thermodynamics: An Engineering Approach |publisher=[[McGraw-Hill Education]] |isbn=9781259822674 |page=6 |edition=9th}}</ref> For example, in the [[kinetic energy]] (KE) formula, if ''g''<sub>c</sub> = 1 is used, then KE is expressed in [[foot-poundal]]s; but if ''g''<sub>c</sub> = 32.174 is used, then KE is expressed in [[foot-pound]]s.

==Motivations==
According to [[Newton's second law]], the [[force]] ''F'' is proportional to the product of mass ''m'' and acceleration ''a'':
:<math>F \propto ma </math>
or
:<math>F = K ma</math>

If ''F'' = 1 [[pound-force|lbf]], ''m'' = 1 [[pound mass|lb]], and ''a'' = {{val|32.174|ul=ft/s2}}, then
:<math>1~\text{lbf} = K \cdot 1~\text{lb} \cdot 32.174~\frac{\text{ft}}{\text{s}^2}</math>
Leading to
:<math>K = \frac{1~\text{lbf}}{1~\text{lb} \cdot 32.174~\frac{\text{ft}}{\text{s}^2}} = 0.03108~\frac{\text{lbf} \cdot \text{s}^2}{\text{lb} \cdot \text{ft}} </math>

''g''<sub>c</sub> is defined as the [[multiplicative inverse|reciprocal]] of the constant ''K''
:<math>g_\text{c} = \frac{1}{K} = 32.174~\frac{\text{lb} \cdot\text{ft}}{\text{lbf} \cdot \text{s}^2}</math>
or equivalently, as
:<math>g_\text{c} = \frac{ma}{F}</math>
